passage:
Uday had been saying "fine" all evening in their Hyderabad flat. Fine about dinner, fine about the weekend plan, fine about her mother visiting. He put the plates down a little too hard. He answered her messages with a single thumbs-up. Pallavi noticed the way he sighed when she mentioned Sunday.
She could have asked, "What's your problem?" Instead she sat on the arm of the sofa. "I think I might have missed something," she said. "You seem annoyed, and I'd really rather hear it straight than guess. I won't be upset if it's about me."
Uday looked at the TV for a while. Then: "You said yes to your mother's visit without asking me. It's the third weekend in a row."
Pallavi nodded. "That's fair. Let's plan the next one together."
His shoulders dropped. Later he even laughed at something on the TV.

qa.q: What did Uday answer Pallavi's messages with?
qa.a: A single thumbs-up.

qa.q: What does Uday putting the plates down too hard suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Irritated about something he hadn't said, with the annoyance leaking out through small actions.

qa.q: Which choice of Pallavi's made directness safe for Uday?
qa.a: Saying she might have missed something and would rather hear it straight, and promising not to be upset, instead of asking 'What's your problem?'

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Uday finally said what was wrong?
qa.a: Probably relieved to hear it straight, and ready to own her part, since she said 'That's fair' and offered to plan the next visit together.

grounding: A woman senses her husband's veiled irritation, says she may have missed something and welcomes a straight answer, and the tension eases.

passage:
On the steps of their parents' house:
"Kishore, you've been 'busy' every time I call about Papa's hospital bills."
"I'm swamped at work, bhaiya."
"You sent the money for his medicines with a note: 'As ALWAYS, happy to help.'"
"Just a joke."
"Hmm." Ujjwal sat down beside him. "Kishore, I think I might have missed something. It sounds like you're annoyed with me, and I'd honestly rather hear it straight. I won't argue back. I'll just listen."
A long silence.
"...Fine. You decide everything about Papa's treatment and just send me the bill. Like I'm a cash machine, not his son."
"Okay." Ujjwal breathed out. "That's fair. I didn't ask you. From now on we decide together. Can you come to the doctor's with us on Saturday?"
"...Yeah. I'll come."

qa.q: What did Kishore write on the note with the medicine money?
qa.a: "As ALWAYS, happy to help."

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel like 'a cash machine, not his son'?
qa.a: He felt shut out of decisions about Papa's treatment and only asked for money, which left him hurt and resentful.

qa.q: What choice of Ujjwal's brought the real issue out?
qa.a: Saying he might have missed something and promising to listen without arguing, then agreeing to decide together and inviting Kishore to the doctor's.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt on first seeing 'ALWAYS' in capitals?
qa.a: Stung and puzzled, sensing hidden anger, but he chose curiosity instead of hitting back.

grounding: An older brother senses veiled irritation in his brother's notes, gently invites the straight version, and the real grievance comes out.

passage:
I noticed it first in Jomon's emails: "Per my last email", "As previously mentioned", "Just circling back for the third time". Polite words with teeth. At stand-up he'd say, "Great, love that," in a voice that meant the opposite. I had been team lead for two months, and he had been passed over for the post.
I could have ignored it, or matched his tone. Instead, one afternoon I asked him to have tea with me in the canteen. I said, "Jomon, I think I might have missed something with you. If you're annoyed with me or with how things are running, I'd rather hear it straight. You won't get in trouble for it."
He looked surprised. Then he told me: I had changed his reporting format without asking. Small, but it stung, on top of the promotion. I changed it back. His emails got shorter after that. I'm Seema, and I still use that sentence.

qa.q: Which phrases did Jomon use in his emails?
qa.a: "Per my last email", "As previously mentioned" and "Just circling back for the third time".

qa.q: What might Jomon have been feeling beneath the polite emails?
qa.a: Stung that his reporting format was changed without asking, on top of being passed over, and unsure it was safe to say so.

qa.q: Which choice of Seema's made directness possible?
qa.a: Inviting Jomon for tea and saying Seema might have missed something, welcoming a straight answer with no trouble attached.

qa.q: What would have changed if Seema had matched Jomon's tone?
qa.a: The sniping would likely have grown, and Seema might never have learned about the reporting format or fixed it.

grounding: A team lead senses veiled irritation from a colleague, gently says they may have missed something and invites a direct answer.

passage:
Project coordinator's note, Vandana, Wednesday
For a week Madhuri's messages have had an edge. "Sure, whatever works for YOU." "Noted. As always." In Monday's call she said, "Great, another change, love that," with a smile that didn't match. She's still doing all her work, on time. But something's off.
I could have ignored it or answered the tone. Instead, after today's call I asked her to stay back for two minutes.
I said, "Madhuri, I think I've missed something here. I'd rather hear it straight from you than guess. Is something I've done bothering you?"
She hesitated, then it came out: I had moved her client presentation to Friday without asking, twice, and she'd had to cancel taking her mother to a hospital appointment. "I didn't want to seem difficult."
I apologised, and we agreed: no schedule changes without asking her first. She laughed, properly this time. "Thank you for asking."
Next: check with the rest of the team about schedule changes.

qa.q: What had Vandana done twice without asking?
qa.a: Moved Madhuri's client presentation to Friday.

qa.q: Why had Madhuri's irritation come out in edged messages instead of plain words?
qa.a: Madhuri didn't want to seem difficult, so the anger about the schedule changes leaked out sideways in sarcastic lines.

qa.q: What did Vandana's words "I think I've missed something here" do well?
qa.a: They took responsibility gently and made a straight answer safe, so Madhuri could name the real problem and they could agree on a fix.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had snapped back at the tone?
qa.a: Madhuri would likely have become more guarded, the schedule problem would have stayed hidden, and the edge in the messages would probably have grown.

grounding: Shows an adult who senses a colleague's veiled irritation, says gently that something may have been missed, and welcomes a direct answer, which ends the sarcasm.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm
Jaya's been prickly all week. "Oh, don't get up, I'll do the groceries again, it's my hobby." Tonight, when I said I'd be late on Saturday, she said, "Of course. Your schedule is the important one." Then she smiled and went to her room.
My first instinct was to be prickly back. Instead I knocked. I said, "Jaya, I think I've missed something, and I'd really rather you just told me. I won't get defensive." (I tried very hard not to.)
She sat on her bed for a long time. Then it came out: since I started the new job, she's done every grocery run and paid the electricity bill twice, and I hadn't noticed. She was angry but didn't want to "make it a big thing".
Fair. Completely fair. We made a list on the back of a receipt, and I'm doing Saturday's shopping before I go out.
She hugged me. The prickliness just went.
Uma

qa.q: What did Jaya say when Uma mentioned being late on Saturday?
qa.a: "Of course. Your schedule is the important one."

qa.q: Why had Jaya's anger come out as prickly remarks?
qa.a: Jaya was angry about doing every grocery run and paying the bill twice, but didn't want to "make it a big thing", so it came out sideways.

qa.q: What choice did Uma make instead of being prickly back?
qa.a: Uma knocked, said something might have been missed, and promised not to get defensive, which made it safe for Jaya to speak plainly.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt once the list was made?
qa.a: Jaya probably felt heard and relieved, since the unfairness was finally noticed and fixed, so the prickly remarks lost their purpose 🤍

grounding: Illustrates an adult who notices a flatmate's veiled irritation and gently invites the straight version, after which the indirect anger fades.
